newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Marsalis conjures soul from slavery.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Marsalis conjures soul from slavery.

text.p: Wynton Marsalis -- trumpet virtuoso, composer and, at 35, one of the world's best-known jazzmen -- sat down at the piano in the corner of his Manhattan apartment the other day and began playing the blues.
He was wearing warmup pants and a sweat shirt, casual for a man who changed jazz presentation more than a decade ago when he showed up on stage in sharp, tailored suits.

Playing a few chords as the sun streamed through the windows of his high-rise overlooking the Hudson River, Marsalis appeared relaxed despite a hectic schedule, and after a chorus or two of the blues he was eager to talk about his new work, "Blood on the Fields."

Perhaps his most ambitious piece to date, the three-hour oratorio with a jazz orchestra tells the story of a slave couple from their journey out of Africa to their struggles to be free and the spiritual lessons learned along the way.
Marsalis, as the work makes evident, is not one to shy away from the big themes. Indeed, his brashness gives much of his music its strength.

"Blood on the Fields" debuted in April 1994 as a commissioned work for Jazz at Lincoln Centre, where Marsalis serves as artistic director, but the composer said it was finished hastily and he has since refined it.
He is now taking it on the road on a U.S.-European tour that began in late January in New Haven, Connecticut, and ends in mid-March in London.

The work deals with many themes -- the danger of pride and the importance of humility, the redemptive power of love, the beauty of America and the brutality of its race relations -- all within the context of slavery. But Marsalis said, "It's not so much about slavery as what goes on today."
For Marsalis, much of what it takes to triumph in both a spiritual and material sense has to do with "soul" -- a concept that in his words comes down to "addressing adversity with elegance."

"To learn how to sing with soul -- that means you understand you have to participate in something, it's your effort," he said. "You don't allow your tragedy to be magnified in the world -- you transform your tragedy into something useful, that's optimistic. That's the whole proposition of soul."

What so many people had misunderstood about the blues, he said, was that it was not a music of tragedy and suffering but the expression of artists surmounting their difficulties. Louis Armstrong, for example, overcame extreme poverty to become a jazz great, his horn a beacon of joy.

Marsalis often tells stories or recounts bits of literature to make a point. In his compositions, crying trumpets, languid trombones or a deep bass line play the same role. His works owe much to the legacy of Duke Ellington and Charles Mingus, whose work he has often performed at the head of the Lincoln Centre Jazz Orchestra.

But "Blood on the Fields" also relies on the talents of singers Cassandra Wilson, recognised as one of the great contemporary jazz singers, and Jon Hendricks, who put words to bebop and changed the art of jazz singing in the 1950s.
The final role is sung by Miles Griffith, a young jazz singer who comes out of the church.
Hendricks, who appeared with the Ellington Orchestra in 1964 for its "Sacred Concerts," said he had not done anything similar until he worked with Marsalis.
"For me it's like performing with Duke all over again," Hendricks said before a rehearsal in New Haven. "I think he captured all of it -- the voicings, tone and colour and shading that Duke used."
